title: Linear attention learns linear dynamical systems
one_liner: A single layer that blends observations (linear attention: when its weights are tuned right) can learn to predict sequences that follow fixed motion rules, doing exactly what a classical algorithm does.
lead: Real systems change over time following patterns: temperature drifts, stock prices trend, pendulums swing. A linear dynamical system is a math way to say this: each new state is a fixed combination of the previous states plus some noise. Modern AI models use a technique for reading sequences (transformers: a model that processes one observation at a time and learns patterns from the order) with a simplified version (linear attention: a way to blend observations by assigning each one a weight or strength) to predict what comes next. This paper proves that when you set up this blending correctly, it learns exactly the same way a classical numerical algorithm does, making it as smart as the optimal method for this problem.

problem.h2: Why can a neural net learn real-world sequences?
paras: Imagine you watch a system evolving: each measurement is a noisy snapshot of a hidden state. The state does not change randomly; it follows a pattern. The position of a pendulum, tomorrow's temperature, a robot's coordinates—all follow predictable motion rules. The optimal way to predict the next state is called a Kalman filter: it keeps track of a belief about the current state and updates that belief each time a new noisy measurement arrives.

Modern neural networks use transformers, which predict sequences by reading all past observations at once. A simpler version called linear attention skips some complexity, but it is still not obvious why it would be as good as a Kalman filter. In real data, measurements do not arrive all at once; they come one at a time, and the world does not repeat perfectly. So the question is: if a neural net only sees one window of past data at a time (not an infinite history), can linear attention learn the same strategy a Kalman filter uses?

callout.html: Linear attention with the right weights predicts sequences by running an iterative update process (Gradient Descent: a way to nudge a guess by moving it toward what the data shows), the same way a classical algorithm does.

paras: The paper specifies the exact values for the attention weights in a single layer that allow it to solve this problem, because these weights encode the optimal update rule from classical optimization theory. Instead of training these weights by trial and error, the paper derives them mathematically from the Kalman filter equations. This is the core insight: you do not need to search; there is one right answer, and it comes from solving the least-squares fitting problem.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: update step size
hidden.name: how much to nudge the prediction
paras: Every time a new measurement arrives, you must decide: should the old prediction change a lot or a little? The update step size (sometimes called the learning rate) controls this. If it is too small, you ignore new information. If it is too large, you overreact to noise. The Kalman filter solves this perfectly by balancing the trust in the old belief against the noise level.

This paper shows that linear attention's weights encode exactly this balance. The weights automatically compute the right step size for each state dimension, using only the information in the recent observations and their noise patterns.

heat.caption: Darker weight means stronger influence on the update step; highlighted weights correspond to the optimal update.

reads.html: The step size is the fraction of the error you use to correct your belief.
The paper proves the set of attention weights computes the optimal solution to the least-squares regression problem (fitting a line through noisy points to minimize total gap) over the window.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: equivalence to Gradient Descent
paras: Here is the core finding: when you set up linear attention a certain way, the output is mathematically identical to taking one step of Gradient Descent. Gradient Descent is the standard algorithm for tweaking a guess to reduce error. In this case, the guess is a linear model (a simple formula) for the next state, and the error comes from not matching the recent observations.

The paper proves this works in two steps. First, for a small window (just two recent observations), the math is exact: the attention weights compute the one gradient descent step that best balances the two observations given their noise levels. Second, for larger windows, experiments suggest the method connects to an advanced version called Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient, which solves the same problem even more skillfully by using information from the whole history. In both cases, the neural net is doing classical optimization, not learning some separate trick.

math.words: prediction equals the sum of past observations each multiplied by an attention weight
symbols: the attention weight for observation at time t

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the system is a position that drifts. We see two recent noisy measurements: z_1 = 10, z_2 = 12.

Kalman filter theory says: if the noise is the same level both times, and the system follows position = previous position + small random drift, then the best next prediction balances both: w_1 = 0.4, w_2 = 0.6.
This is one Gradient Descent step toward fitting the observations: it nudges the estimate by 10% of the gap (from the old guess of 10 toward the average 11).

math.note: The weights are not learned by trial and error; the paper computes them from the noise levels using calculus.

bars.h2: Prediction accuracy on real dynamical systems

charts.title: Naive approach: ignore noise patterns
charts.note: Without reasoning about noise, the model overfits or ignores signal.

charts.title: This paper: linear attention with right weights
charts.note: Matching the Kalman filter method, the model generalizes to unseen sequences.

items.html: If the true noise variance is wrong, the weights are wrong. The method assumes you can estimate noise from the data.
This theory only covers linear systems where the state evolves as a fixed linear combination. Real pendulums and robots have nonlinear dynamics, so the method breaks down.
The paper proves the small-window case exactly and hypothesizes the larger-window behavior; experiments confirm the Conjugate Gradient connection, but the full theory is incomplete.

items.b: Done right: noise is estimated, system is linear.
items.html: When the assumptions hold, the neural net recovers the classical algorithm exactly, requiring no gradient-based training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate a synthetic linear dynamical system (e.g., position with constant drift and noise). Train a transformer with linear attention on noisy observations. Compute the learned attention weights and compare them to the theoretical weights from Kalman filter theory. Show that they match, and that the network's next-step predictions are as accurate as the classical algorithm.
demo.metric_eq: prediction error = mean squared difference between learned attention output and Kalman filter prediction
demo.closing: The neural net and the classical algorithm should produce nearly identical predictions, proving the theory: linear attention encodes Gradient Descent.
